# Education Investment vs. Outcomes: 30-Country Comparison

## Overview
This dataset compiles education-related metrics for 30 countries spanning Europe, Asia, the Americas, and Oceania. It pairs public education spending with three outcome dimensions — academic performance, tertiary access, and youth labor market integration — to enable cross-country comparison.

## Data Source

### education_spending
One row per country. Fields: `country` (string, country name), `region` (string, broad geographic grouping), `edu_spending_pct_gdp` (float, public education expenditure as % of GDP, range ~2.9–7.2%). Based on OECD/World Bank estimates circa 2022.

### pisa_scores
One row per country. Fields: `country` (string), `pisa_avg` (integer, average of reading, math, and science scores from PISA 2022, range 379–561).

### tertiary_enrollment
One row per country. Fields: `country` (string), `enrollment_rate` (integer, gross tertiary enrollment as % of the relevant age cohort, range 43–110%). Values above 100% are possible due to mature-age and international students.

### youth_unemployment
One row per country. Fields: `country` (string), `youth_unemp_rate` (float, unemployment rate for ages 15–24 as % of youth labor force, range ~4.1–30.2%). Data circa 2022–2023.

## Data Notes
- All four datasets share the same 30 countries and are joinable on the `country` field.
- Gross enrollment rates can exceed 100% due to inclusion of students outside the typical age cohort.
- PISA scores represent a combined average; individual subject scores may differ.
- Youth unemployment definitions follow ILO standards but national measurement practices may vary slightly.

Cross-Country Analysis · Education Systems · 2022

Education Investment vs. Outcomes

Spending more on education does not guarantee better outcomes. Across 30 countries, the relationship between public education expenditure and academic performance, university access, and youth labor market integration reveals striking non-linearities and efficiency gaps.

PISA 2022 · World Bank · OECD 30 Countries · 4 Metrics
Spending range
2.9–7.2%
of GDP on education
PISA spread
182 pts
Singapore (561) to Brazil (379)
Youth unemployment
4–30%
Japan (4.1%) to Costa Rica (30.2%)
Enrollment range
43–110%
Mexico (43%) to Australia/Greece

Spending, PISA Score, Enrollment & Youth Unemployment

Each bubble is one country. X-axis = education spending as % of GDP. Y-axis = average PISA 2022 score. Bubble size = tertiary enrollment rate. Bubble color = youth unemployment rate (green = low, red = high). Labels mark notable cases.

Youth unemployment: Low (4%) High (30%)
Bubble size = tertiary enrollment:
Low (43%)
Medium (70%)
High (110%)
Efficiency outliers

High outcomes, moderate spending

These countries achieve top PISA scores and low youth unemployment despite spending less than 5% of GDP — illustrating that institutional quality and curriculum efficiency matter more than raw investment.

Singapore (2.9%) Japan (3.2%) Ireland (3.5%) South Korea (4.5%) Estonia (5.2%)
High spend, mixed results

Heavy investors with divergent outcomes

Sweden (7.2%), Norway (6.6%), and Brazil (6.1%) all spend well above average on education, yet show notably different PISA scores and youth unemployment rates — spending alone cannot explain performance.

Sweden (7.2% GDP) Costa Rica (7.0%) Norway (6.6%) Brazil (6.1%) Israel (6.2%)
Labor market disconnect

Education investment ≠ job access

Spain, Greece, and Italy all maintain mid-range spending yet face youth unemployment rates of 23–28%. Meanwhile Japan and Germany achieve near-full youth employment at similar or lower spending. Vocational pathways and structural labor factors dominate.

Spain (28.4% youth unemp) Greece (27.2%) Italy (23.7%) Japan (4.1%) Germany (5.8%)
PISA Score vs. Youth Unemployment
Higher academic scores do not guarantee lower youth unemployment
Education Spending vs. Youth Unemployment
No clear linear relationship — high spenders span the full unemployment range
Data sources: PISA 2022 (OECD), World Bank EdStats (education spending, tertiary enrollment, circa 2022), ILO/World Bank youth unemployment (2022–2023). Gross enrollment rates above 100% reflect inclusion of mature-age and international students. PISA scores are averages of reading, mathematics, and science domains. All country-level data are the most recent available estimates.
